anodal_tdcs.name: Anodal tDCS (Left Temporoparietal)
anodal_tdcs.short_description: Anodal tDCS to left temporoparietal cortex applied during concurrent behavioural therapy to boost cortical excitability and augment LTP- like plasticity; efficacy moderated by BDNF Val66Met genotype.

auditory_temporal_processing.name: Rapid auditory temporal processing (40-Hz FM detection)
auditory_temporal_processing.units: FM detection threshold (modulation index); lower values = better performance (inverse scale)

bdnf_val66met.name: BDNF Val66Met genotype (rs6265)
bdnf_val66met.units: genotype category: val/val (typical) vs Met-allele carrier (atypical)

bilateral_middle_frontal_gyrus_recovery.name: Bilateral Middle Frontal Gyrus and Right Temporo-Occipital MTG — Fluency Recovery

cognitive_linguistic_treatment.name: Cognitive-Linguistic Treatment
cognitive_linguistic_treatment.short_description: Impairment-based treatment targeting specific linguistic functions (e.g., semantics via BOX or phonology via FIKS) to improve word finding.

communicative_shaping.name: Communicative Shaping
communicative_shaping.short_description: Graded increase in verbal demand within structured communicative tasks, reinforcing successive approximations toward more complex propositional speech.

constraint_induced_aphasia_therapy.name: Constraint-Induced Aphasia Therapy (CIAT / CILT)
constraint_induced_aphasia_therapy.short_description: A therapeutic technique requiring intense massed practice of speech acts in a communicative environment, constraining the use of non-verbal communication strategies.

inhibitory_rtms.name: Inhibitory rTMS (Right Pars Triangularis / BA45)
inhibitory_rtms.short_description: Slow (1 Hz) inhibitory rTMS to right pars triangularis to suppress maladaptive right IFG overactivity, reducing transcallosal inhibition of left perilesional language cortex and improving naming fluency.

intensive_aphasia_therapy.name: Intensive Aphasia Therapy (Early Acute)
intensive_aphasia_therapy.short_description: High-intensity aphasia rehabilitation delivered within the first 14 days post-stroke.

intensive_speech_and_language_therapy.name: Intensive Speech and Language Therapy
intensive_speech_and_language_therapy.short_description: High-intensity speech and language therapy (>=10h/week) combining linguistic and communicative-pragmatic approaches.

intention_treatment.name: Intention Treatment
intention_treatment.short_description: A naming treatment where trials are initiated with complex left-hand movements to engage right-hemisphere intentional mechanisms.

left_anterior_temporal_lobe__Robson2014.name: Left Anterior Temporal Lobe (Residual Comprehension Substrate in Wernicke's Aphasia)

left_arcuate_fasciculus_slf.name: Left Arcuate Fasciculus and Superior Longitudinal Fascicle (Dorsal Language Pathway)

aliases: left periinsular white matter (medial to insula, lateral to basal ganglia)
Posterior limb of internal capsule L
Posterior limb of internal capsule left
Anterior limb of internal capsule L
Anterior limb of internal capsule left
left_frontal_white_matter_bottleneck.name: Left Frontal White Matter Bottleneck

left_ifg_pars_opercularis.name: Left IFG Pars Opercularis (Broca's area, dorsal stream hub)

left_ifg_pars_orbitalis.name: Left Inferior Frontal Gyrus Pars Orbitalis

left_middle_temporal_gyrus.name: Left Middle Temporal Gyrus (Ventral Stream Node)

left_posterior_temporal_white_matter_bot.name: Left Posterior Temporal White Matter Bottleneck

left_precentral_gyrus_insula.name: Left precentral gyrus of the insula

left_presma_dacc.name: Left Presupplementary Motor Area / Dorsal Anterior Cingulate Cortex

left_superior_temporal_gyrus.name: Left Superior Temporal Gyrus (Dorsal Stream Node)

left_superior_temporal_gyrus__Leff2009.name: Left Posterior Superior Temporal Gyrus and Sulcus (Auditory STM / Comprehension Shared Substrate)

left_superior_temporal_gyrus_wernicke.name: Left Superior Temporal Gyrus (Wernicke's Area and Planum Temporale)

left_superior_temporal_gyrus_wernickes.name: Left Superior Temporal Gyrus (Wernicke's region, mid-posterior)

left_supramarginal_gyrus_premotor.name: Left Supramarginal Gyrus and Premotor Cortex (supra-Sylvian)

aliases: basal portion of left temporal lobe
left_temporobasal__Goldenberg1994.name: Left Temporobasal Cortex (basal temporal lobe / entorhinal–perisylvian junction)

lesion_volume__Goldenberg1994.name: Total lesion volume as predictor of recovery and therapy gain (Goldenberg & Spatt 1994)

listen_repeat_cycle.name: Listen–Repeat–Spell–Copy–Spell Cycle
listen_repeat_cycle.short_description: Five-step training cycle (listen → repeat → spell → copy → re-spell) that combines phonological activation with errorless encoding and retrieval practice to strengthen phonological-to-orthographic conversion.

massed_practice.name: Massed Practice
massed_practice.short_description: High-frequency, concentrated repetition of target behaviours across sessions. A dose parameter shared across CIAT, MIT, and Spell-Study- Spell that drives activity-dependent plasticity in perilesional cortex.

melodic_intonation_therapy.name: Melodic Intonation Therapy (MIT)
melodic_intonation_therapy.short_description: A language production treatment for severe nonfluent aphasia involving repetitive singing of short sentences combined with rhythmic hand tapping.

melodic_intoning.name: Melodic Intoning
melodic_intoning.short_description: Singing target utterances on two pitches with exaggerated prosody and progressive fading of clinician support; the core procedure of MIT that recruits right-hemisphere speech-motor pathways.

phonological_component_analysis.name: Phonological Component Analysis (PCA)
phonological_component_analysis.short_description: A phonologically based naming treatment modeled after Semantic Feature Analysis (SFA) where patients identify rhymes, first/final sounds, first sound associates, and syllable counts for target items.

phonological_feature_analysis.name: Phonological Feature Analysis
phonological_feature_analysis.short_description: Systematic picture-cued analysis of a target word's first phoneme, final phoneme, syllable count, rhyme, and phoneme-sharing word to strengthen lexical-phonological retrieval via spreading activation.

retrieval_practice.name: Retrieval Practice
retrieval_practice.short_description: Active recall attempts before feedback, exploiting the testing effect to strengthen long-term retention of trained word forms beyond what restudy alone achieves.

rhythmic_hand_tapping.name: Rhythmic Left-Hand Tapping
rhythmic_hand_tapping.short_description: Left-hand rhythmic tapping on each syllable, co-occurring with melodic intoning to engage right somatomotor cortex and provide temporal cueing for articulatory onset.

right_ifg_pars_opercularis.name: Right Inferior Frontal Gyrus Pars Opercularis

right_ifg_pars_triangularis.name: Right Inferior Frontal Gyrus Pars Triangularis

semantic_feature_analysis.name: Semantic Feature Analysis
semantic_feature_analysis.short_description: A treatment that guides the client to produce semantically related features of a target word to strengthen the semantic network and improve lexical retrieval.

semantic_feature_generation.name: Semantic Feature Generation
semantic_feature_generation.short_description: Guided generation of semantic features (category, function, properties, location, association) for a pictured target, driving spreading activation through the semantic network to support lexical retrieval.

spell_study_spell.name: Spell-study-spell training
spell_study_spell.short_description: An impairment-based treatment for acquired dysgraphia in which patients listen to a target word, repeat it, spell it, copy it, and spell it again, working through a pre-determined individually tailored 40-word list. Emphasizes listening and repetition alongside the spelling task.

stroke_severity_sss.name: Neurological stroke severity (Scandinavian Stroke Scale)
stroke_severity_sss.units: score 0–58 (SSS) or 0–42 (modified SSS); higher score = less severe impairment

tdcs_aphasia_treatment.name: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) during aphasia treatment
tdcs_aphasia_treatment.short_description: Non-invasive brain stimulation using low-intensity electrical current to modulate cortical excitability during speech therapy.

tms_right_ifg.name: Inhibitory rTMS to Right Inferior Frontal Gyrus
tms_right_ifg.short_description: Low-frequency (1 Hz) inhibitory repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation applied to the right posterior inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis) to reduce maladaptive right-hemisphere overactivation.

tms_right_ifg__Naeser2005.name: Inhibitory rTMS to Right Pars Triangularis (BA45) for Anomia in Nonfluent Aphasia
tms_right_ifg__Naeser2005.short_description: Open-protocol pilot study applying slow (1 Hz) inhibitory repetitive TMS daily for 10 days to the right pars triangularis (anterior Broca homologue, BA45), aiming to suppress maladaptive right hemisphere overactivation in chronic nonfluent aphasia and thereby improve picture naming. First study to demonstrate lasting naming benefit (2 and 8 months post-rTMS). n=4 chronic aphasia patients, 5–11 years post-stroke.

treatment_of_underlying_forms.name: Treatment of Underlying Forms (TUF)
treatment_of_underlying_forms.short_description: A linguistic-specific treatment that uses active forms of target sentences to train the comprehension and production of noncanonical structures by focusing on the underlying linguistic operations (e.g., movement).

typicality_ordering.name: Typicality-Based Training Order
typicality_ordering.short_description: Sequencing training items from most to least typical within a semantic category to exploit prototype effects and stabilise semantic attractors before training peripheral category members.

typicality_semantic_feature_analysis.name: Typicality-based Semantic Feature Analysis (SFA)
typicality_semantic_feature_analysis.short_description: A semantic-based treatment that improves naming by having patients generate semantic features of a target object using a structured chart.

verb_argument_structure_training.name: Verb Argument Structure Training
verb_argument_structure_training.short_description: Meta-linguistic training of verb argument structure and thematic- syntactic mapping using complex (non-canonical) sentence structures; drives generalisation to simpler structures via CATE and recruits right-hemisphere syntactic networks.

verbal_constraint.name: Verbal Constraint
verbal_constraint.short_description: Complete prohibition of gesture and non-verbal compensatory strategies, forcing the patient to use verbal communication exclusively during CIAT sessions.

virtual_reality_rehabilitation.name: Virtual Reality Rehabilitation
virtual_reality_rehabilitation.short_description: Use of computer-generated environments (immersive or non-immersive) to provide interactive, goal-oriented tasks for stroke recovery.

Participants (N = 138 PPA, N = 37 acute stroke) completed the BNT and HANA. A subset of participants (N = 31 PPA, N = 37 acute stroke) provided neuroimaging data.

Technicians blinded to the behavioural results used MRIcron to trace areas of tissue disfunction, defined as areas of dense ischemia/infarct that were bright on DWI maps but dark on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps. Traced lesions were coregistered to T1 scans using SPM12. Lesioned tissue was replaced with tissue from the undamaged right hemisphere.

Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression was used to evaluate which ROIs were related to behaviour on object and action naming. LASSO regression with standardised features was instantiated with the glmnet package in R, using leave-one-out cross-validation to select the λ value that resulted in the minimum mean cross validated error.

The sample consisted of 43 women and 56 men, 48 African Americans and 51 Caucasians. They averaged 58 years of age (s.d. ¼ 11; range ¼ 26–79), 14 years of education (s.d. ¼ 3; range ¼ 10–21) and 53 months post onset of stroke (s.d. ¼ 68; range ¼ 1–381).

VLSM analysis was performed by running a simple regression analysis at each voxel, with the lesion status as the independent variable and the factor score as the dependent variable. To control the effect of total lesion volume, each lesion map was normalized to have a unit norm.

The derived statistical p-map was thresholded with FDR q ¼ 0.05 (Semantic Recognition factor was thresholded with FDR q ¼ 0.1) and isolated clusters with voxel number no more than 50 after thresholding were removed.
High-resolution whole-brain T1-weighted images (magnetization- prepared rapid acquisition gradient echo) were acquired for the 50 participants undergoing MRI.

source_passages.quote: Regression analyses showed that arcuate fasciculus lesion load, but not extreme capsule or uncinate fasciculus lesion load or overall lesion size, significantly predicted rate, informativeness, and overall efficiency of speech as well as naming ability.

A regression analysis was first conducted using lesion size and lesion loads of all 3 tracts (ie, AF, EmC, and UF) as predictors of words/min (adjusted R²=0.301, P=0.011). AF lesion load proved to be the best variable (partial R²=0.175, P=0.030; Figure 2A), whereas EmC lesion load (partial R²=0.087, P=0.135), UF lesion load (partial R²=0.098, P=0.112), and lesion size (partial R²=0.002, P=0.829) were shown to be nonsignificant predictors.

The study group consisted of 30 right-handed patients, all of whom had left-hemispheric strokes in the middle cerebral artery territory and were at least 11 months post stroke at the time of testing (6 females and 24 males; mean age 58.5 years [SD 10.0]; mean time poststroke 35.0 months [SD 28.7]).

The control subjects underwent diffusion tensor imaging using a single-shot, spin-echo echoplanar imaging sequence with the following parameters: TR=10 seconds; TE=86.9 ms; resolution 2.6×2.6×2.6 mm³; 30 noncollinear diffusion directions with a b-value of 1000 s/mm²; and 6 acquisitions with a value of 0 s/mm².

source_passages.quote: Regression analyses showed that arcuate fasciculus lesion load, but not extreme capsule or uncinate fasciculus lesion load or overall lesion size, significantly predicted rate, informativeness, and overall efficiency of speech as well as naming ability.

A regression analysis was first conducted using lesion size and lesion loads of all 3 tracts (ie, AF, EmC, and UF) as predictors of words/min (adjusted R²=0.301, P=0.011). AF lesion load proved to be the best variable (partial R²=0.175, P=0.030; Figure 2A), whereas EmC lesion load (partial R²=0.087, P=0.135), UF lesion load (partial R²=0.098, P=0.112), and lesion size (partial R²=0.002, P=0.829) were shown to be nonsignificant predictors.

The study group consisted of 30 right-handed patients, all of whom had left-hemispheric strokes in the middle cerebral artery territory and were at least 11 months post stroke at the time of testing (6 females and 24 males; mean age 58.5 years [SD 10.0]; mean time poststroke 35.0 months [SD 28.7]).

The control subjects underwent diffusion tensor imaging using a single-shot, spin-echo echoplanar imaging sequence with the following parameters: TR=10 seconds; TE=86.9 ms; resolution 2.6×2.6×2.6 mm³; 30 noncollinear diffusion directions with a b-value of 1000 s/mm²; and 6 acquisitions with a value of 0 s/mm².

source_passages.quote: For the AF, a curved fiber bundle that connects the posterior portion of the temporoparietal junction with the frontal cortex, we drew 1 region of interest on the Fractional Anisotropy (FA) map in the white matter underlying the posterior middle and superior temporal gyri at approximately x=−50 mm (MNI space); a second region of interest was drawn on the same sagittal slice in the white matter underlying the pars opercularis of the posterior inferior frontal gyrus.

source_passages.quote: The binary fiber tracts of the 10 healthy control subjects were summed to generate a fiber map using Matlab (Figure 1). Voxel intensities ranged from I=0 (ie, voxel is not part of the tract in any of the subjects) to I=10 (ie, voxel is part of the tract in all 10 subjects); thus, the probability that a particular voxel would be part of the tract was calculated as one tenth of the voxel's intensity.
Thirty patients with chronic stroke with residual impairments in speech production underwent high-resolution anatomic MRI and a battery of cognitive and language tests.

source_passages.quote: VLSM of the Speech Recognition factor identiﬁed a parallel region inferior to the Sylvian ﬁssure, primarily in the superior temporal gyrus, including prominent involvement in Wernicke's area and extending deep into planum temporale (Fig. 4, red–yellow).

Together, these two factors map the classic peri-Sylvian language regions and the superior-inferior division between production and recognition provides new evidence to reﬁne the dorsal–ventral division in dual-pathway models of speech processing.

Our ﬁndings support the involvement of planum temporale and Wernicke's area in speech recognition, but as components of the ventral route, which our VLSM of Speech Recognition locates deep and inferior to the Sylvian ﬁssure along the length of the superior temporal gyrus.

This localization of the ventral route converges with a recent meta-analysis of functional neuroimaging studies that localized speech recognition processes to the superior temporal gyrus and revealed a posterior-to-anterior progression from recognition of speech sounds to spoken words in the superior temporal lobe.

The third factor had high loadings from auditory lexical decision and phoneme discrimination tests, and moderate loadings from rhyme discrimination and word and nonword repetition tests. These tests capture auditory-phonolo- gical perception; hence, we call this factor 'Speech Recognition'.

source_passages.quote: Global aphasia is associated with extensive cortical damage. Middle and inferior frontal gyri, temporal regions (temporal pole; Heschl's and superior temporal gyri), insula and rolandic operculum, pre- and postcentral gyri, and putamen all had high predictive relevance for global aphasia.

Ten participants with chronic aphasia (3 women, mean age = 68.9 ± 10.2) following a single left hemisphere ischemic stroke recruited through local patient association by referral following discharge from rehabilitation centers in the area and following self-referral are included in this study.

Images were acquired using a 3 T MRI Siemens Trio scanner updated to Prisma Fit with a standard 32-channel head coil during data collection. The image sequence is a T2*-weighted pulse sequence (184 volumes; TR = 2200 ms; TE = 30 ms; matrix = 64 × 64 voxels; FOV = 210 mm; flip angle = 90°; slice thickness = 3 mm).

Resting-state functional connectivity analysis was performed using the CONN func- tional connectivity toolbox (v.18.b, available online: http://www.nitrc.org/projects/conn, accessed on 29 January 2021, [63]). source_passages.quote: In both the naming and spelling treatment groups, post-treatment activation was limited to right temporal regions, including the aSTG and temporal pole (for both groups), and the aMTG and pMTG (for the naming treatment group only).

Separate analyses conducted within each group (Table 6) revealed a signiﬁcant increase in activation from pre- to post-treatment (i.e., upregulation) only in the sentence production/comprehension and the spelling treatment groups, and no changes between time points for the naming treatment group or for the natural history (no treatment) group.
No associations were found in the spelling treatment group (Table 7).

Upregulation of right hemisphere homologues of the language network was also observed in the spelling treatment group. This ﬁnding was unexpected, both based on our predictions and on the ﬁndings of previous studies (De Marco et al., 2018; Purcell et al., 2017, 2019), in which evidence of neural plasticity following spelling treatment was found in left perilesional regions.

Importantly, upregulation of activation in this group was not signiﬁcantly associated with performance on word or sentence comprehension, suggesting that activation changes in this group did not result from improved lexical, sentence, or discourse-level comprehension following language intervention. One possible interpretation of these results is that the spelling treatment, which also emphasized listening and repetition, may have improved phonological processing, thereby resulting in better discrimination of real speech from reversed speech and increased post-treatment BOLD signal for the Story > Control contrast.

Separate analyses conducted within each group (Table 6) revealed a signiﬁcant increase in activation from pre- to post-treatment (i.e., upregulation) only in the sentence production/comprehension and the spelling treatment groups, and no changes between time points for the naming treatment group or for the natural history (no treatment) group.
No associations were found in the spelling treatment group (Table 7).

Upregulation of right hemisphere homologues of the language network was also observed in the spelling treatment group. This ﬁnding was unexpected, both based on our predictions and on the ﬁndings of previous studies (De Marco et al., 2018; Purcell et al., 2017, 2019), in which evidence of neural plasticity following spelling treatment was found in left perilesional regions.

Importantly, upregulation of activation in this group was not signiﬁcantly associated with performance on word or sentence comprehension, suggesting that activation changes in this group did not result from improved lexical, sentence, or discourse-level comprehension following language intervention. One possible interpretation of these results is that the spelling treatment, which also emphasized listening and repetition, may have improved phonological processing, thereby resulting in better discrimination of real speech from reversed speech and increased post-treatment BOLD signal for the Story > Control contrast.

uncinate_fasciculus.basis: XTRACT label of the same tract. JHU lists an uncinate label, but its 50 %-threshold image has no voxels for it (nor for the cingulum or the temporal SLF), so it could never be damaged.
uncinate_fasciculus.name: Uncinate fasciculus

unmapped.left_extreme_capsule: No atlas used here (JHU, XTRACT) labels the extreme capsule. It carries the inferior fronto-occipital and uncinate fasciculi, but those tracts are not the extreme-capsule fibre system itself, so it is not approximated.
unmapped.left_frontal_white_matter_bottleneck: A "bottleneck" is a region defined in its source paper by the convergence of several tracts, not an atlas structure.
unmapped.left_perisylvian_network: A network, not a single anatomical structure.
unmapped.left_posterior_middle_temporal_white_mat: White matter under the posterior middle temporal gyrus; no tract label.

coverage.need: The inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus has 3 findings; the anterior thalamic radiation (measured by JHU) none. Both were linked to semantic deficits and verbal fluency in stroke cohorts that measured tract damage directly.
3 findings on the inferior temporal gyrus and 5 on the fusiform gyrus, regions often damaged by posterior cerebral artery strokes and relevant to naming and reading.

7 findings, but neither JHU nor XTRACT labels the extreme capsule. Oeckel et al. 2021 and Kümmerer et al. 2013 measured it with tractography-derived templates from healthy subjects; extracting them documents the ventral-stream evidence, and their templates (if shared) would make the region reachable.

3 findings on the supplementary motor area and 1 on the frontal aslant tract (reachable since the XTRACT atlas was added), which connects it to the inferior frontal gyrus and is linked to verbal fluency after stroke.

The insula's role in apraxia of speech rests mainly on Dronkers 1996 (precentral gyrus of the insula) and is disputed: Hillis et al. 2004 placed it in the posterior inferior frontal gyrus instead. The frontal operculum has no finding at all. Both sides should be in the KB.
Every right-hemisphere region has 1-3 findings. Right-hemisphere structure and its role in recovery matter for interpreting a left-hemisphere lesion (and for right-hemisphere or bilateral lesions).

Lesions often reach the thalamus, caudate, putamen and pallidum (AAL measures all four), but the KB has no finding on the thalamus or caudate and 4 findings from one paper on putamen and pallidum (Radanovic & Mansur 2017 was extracted as a narrative review, without region-level findings). The subcortical-aphasia literature also shows that much of it reflects cortical hypoperfusion, which the report should be able to say.
